conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that arthroscopy does not meaningfully help with knee osteoarthritis and strongly recommends against the procedure based on high-quality randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, and clinical guidelines.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**No, arthroscopy does not meaningfully help knee osteoarthritis, and current evidence strongly recommends against it.**

The strongest evidence comes from randomized controlled trials directly testing arthroscopy against sham/placebo surgery. Moseley et al.'s landmark placebo-controlled trial found that arthroscopic surgery (lavage or debridement) provided no better pain relief or functional improvement than a sham procedure in patients with knee osteoarthritis (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259). A follow-up RCT by Kirkley et al. compared arthroscopic surgery plus optimized medical/physical therapy to optimized therapy alone in moderate-to-severe knee OA, concluding "arthroscopic surgery for osteoarthritis of the knee provides no additional benefit to optimized physical and medical therapy" (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0708333).

These findings have been reinforced by systematic reviews and clinical guidelines. A 2017 BMJ Rapid Recommendation, based on a linked systematic review and meta-analysis, issued a **strong recommendation against** arthroscopic surgery for degenerative knee disease (including osteoarthritis and degenerative meniscal tears), stating that further research is unlikely to change this conclusion (https://bjsm.bmj.com/content/52/5/313). A subsequent Cochrane systematic review update similarly concluded that arthroscopic surgery provides little or no clinically important benefit for patients with degenerative knee disease, despite the procedure remaining common in practice (https://www.cochrane.org/th/evidence/CD014328_arthroscopic-surgery-degenerative-knee-disease).

**Conclusion:** Across multiple high-quality RCTs, systematic reviews, and clinical practice guidelines, the evidence consistently shows arthroscopy offers no meaningful benefit over sham surgery, physical therapy, or optimized medical management for knee osteoarthritis, despite its continued widespread use.
